extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists and educated public interested in physics, chemistry, and biology)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observable standards for designing, recording, and interpreting laboratory experiments on combustion and detonation of gaseous mixtures in tubes (including photographic/measurement techniques and diagnostic signs of detonation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between detonation-wave and progressive combustion (Berthelot's 'onde explosive')
rubrics_metrics.description: Berthelot gave the name 'l'onde explosive' (detonation-wave) to the flame travelling with its maximum velocity, thus distinguishing it from the variable progressive combustion which precedes its development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the detonation-wave as a distinct phenomenon with a characteristic constant velocity for each mixture that greatly exceeds the variable progressive combustion rates; report whether a flame has reached this maximum-velocity regime rather than describing only the earlier progressive combustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity of the explosion-wave as a physical constant (approx. equal to sound speed in burning gases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The velocity of the explosion-wave constitutes a physical constant which has a specific value for each inflammable mixture; measurements ... have shown that it is approximately equal to the velocity of sound in the burning gases at the temperature of the explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting measured explosion speeds, compare to the calculated/known velocity of sound in the hot combustion products at the relevant temperature; provide mixture composition and temperature so the comparison is meaningful (example: hydrogen+oxygen in equivalent proportions ≈ 3000 yards/second).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics marking the initiation of a detonation-wave
rubrics_metrics.description: The initiation of the detonation-wave is marked by certain characteristics — (1) a sudden increase in intensity of the flame, accompanied by an instantaneous rise in pressure; (2) rapid and complete combustion; (3) the setting up of a strongly luminous backward wave — the so-called 'retonation-wave' — which under certain conditions travels as rapidly as the detonation-wave itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these observable markers (pressure jump, sudden luminosity increase, complete combustion, backward luminous wave) as diagnostic criteria that detonation has been set up; note that glass tubes often fracture where detonation originates (practical indicator).

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographic recording method for analysing flame and detonation movements (Dixon apparatus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prof. H. B. Dixon's apparatus: drum carrying a narrow strip of Eastman film rotated at ~100 metres/second; the image of the flame is focused onto the vertically moving film producing inclined lines of light representing the combined motions; detonation-wave is represented by a straight line while slower progressive combustion appears as a curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To capture and interpret rapid flame motion, document film speed and geometry of imaging; interpret straight-line traces as constant-velocity (detonation) fronts and curved traces as accelerating progressive combustion; record flash duration (noted <1/100 second) and include reference marks for position calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of flame progression and their observable signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: When gases are ignited at the open end of a long tube, the flame travels for some distance with a uniform slow velocity; it then begins to vibrate, swinging backwards and forwards with oscillations of increasing amplitude; then it either dies down or sometimes the gas detonates. If the gas is fired near the closed end of the tube, the movement of the flame is uniformly accelerated until the detonation is set up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the flame stage (uniform slow motion, oscillatory growth, acceleration to detonation or extinction) and link ignition position relative to tube ends to expected behaviour; include observations of luminosity and completeness of combustion as they change across stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of compression-waves, reflections, and coalescence in flame dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The flame is preceded by an invisible compression-wave which travels with the velocity of sound through the unignited gas and is reflected from the ends of the tube. Reflections can check or assist the flame; stronger reflected waves can overtake weaker ones and coalesce, producing a single wave traversing the tube. As many as one hundred reflections have been counted in such explosions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting flame propagation in confined tubes, record and consider compression-wave reflections and their timing; document any asymmetric behaviour due to differing reflection strengths and the coalescence process that can lead to a dominant travelling wave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of tube length and ignition location on detonation setting distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The detonation-wave is set up only after the flame has run some distance, which depends on the nature of the mixture and on the size of the spark. Le Chatelier's apparatus was not fast enough to analyse the detonation wave itself for very short tubes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report tube length and spark energy; expect a required run-up distance for detonation that varies with mixture composition and ignition energy; for short tubes detonation may not develop within the available column length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of water vapour and mixture purity on ignition and detonation velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dixon showed that an electric spark would fire ordinary electrolytic gas whether in the dried or moist condition, and that the velocity of detonation was practically unaffected by the presence of aqueous vapour. Baker's experiments with very pure hydrogen and oxygen have shown that the initiation of the flame is largely influenced by the purity of the mixture. Dixon and Bradshaw have shown by photographs that the flame, once it has been started by a spark, spreads with the same velocity in the dry as in the moist gases, and undergoes the same changes in intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing initiation and propagation, report gas purity and moisture content separately: moisture may not affect detonation velocity once started, but mixture purity can influence the ease of initiation; include photographic evidence where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression-induced remote ignition in funnel/capillary geometries
rubrics_metrics.description: Dixon and Bradshaw showed that the compression-wave which travels in front of the flame in the initial stage of the explosion may, under certain conditions, bring about the spontaneous inflammation of the gases in a region of the tube some distance from the spark. In a tube with a funnel followed by a short capillary, firing in the middle led almost simultaneously to ignition in the capillary due to sudden pressure increase and heat of compression raising gases to ignition temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In geometries with abrupt area changes (funnels, capillaries), account for local pressure and temperature rises caused by compression-waves as potential causes of remote ignition; describe geometry and include reference marks to locate simultaneous ignition events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of explosion luminosity source
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be observed that the light produced by the explosion is chiefly due to particles knocked from the glass and raised to incandescence; the small particles suspended in the burning gases glow by the heat imparted to them by the hotter but invisible gaseous products of combustion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quantifying luminosity or using light intensity as a proxy for reaction progress, consider particulate contribution (from glass or introduced salts) vs gaseous emission; control for or note presence of particulate sources in photographic/optical diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for classifying spirochetes (bacterial vs protozoan features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffuse nuclei and transverse fission of spirochaetes suggest bacteria, while the presence of an undulating membrane, longitudinal fission, and even definite 'chromosomes' suggest protozoa. Mr. H. B. Fantham leans to the protozoan interpretation based on observed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning taxa, enumerate microscopic/behavioural characters (nuclear appearance, mode of fission, presence/structure of membranes, chromosome-like structures) and discuss how each feature supports bacterial or protozoan classification; include motility analysis (vibratory flexion + spiral corkscrew movement due to myoneme fibrillae) as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of artificial parthenogenesis success (Loeb's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prof. Jacques Loeb induced, by adding to 'hypertonic' sea-water a small quantity of a monobasic fatty acid, the formation in sea-urchin ova of an egg membrane and perfectly normal development in the great majority of the eggs of a given female. The results lead to the conclusion that membrane-formation is connected with the solution or hydrolysis of a layer of fatty material underneath the surface-film of the egg and that the spermatozoon acts as a catalyser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess parthenogenesis methods by (a) whether an egg membrane forms, (b) whether development proceeds normally in the majority of eggs, and (c) whether the induced chemical conditions plausibly mimic spermatozoon action (hydrolysis/liquefaction of fatty material and initiation of oxidation processes). Report concentrations and seawater tonicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature stability measure: code and frozen checklist for common animal names
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee on nomenclature arrived unanimously at a code of rules which would cover 90 per cent of all possible difficulties. The committee resolved to prepare a check-list of some thousands of common animals the names of which were not henceforth to be changed on any pretext whatsoever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For taxonomic/nomenclatural practice, adopt and report adherence to the new code for the covered cases and consult the committee's checklist to avoid unnecessary name changes for common species; document exceptional cases referred to the committee for the remaining difficulties.
